newsitem.title: USA: Empire Blue Cross wants to convert to for-profit.
newsitem.headline: Empire Blue Cross wants to convert to for-profit.

text.p: Medical insurer Empire Blue Cross and Blue Shield, responding to mounting competition in the healthcare industry, said on Thursday that it would seek approval from New York state regulators to convert itself into a for-profit organisation.

The proposal -- which also calls for creation of a charitable foundation to fill the company's traditional role of providing health care for uninsured and poor people -- must be approved by a state court, the state Department of Insurance and the state Attorney General's Office.
Empire Blue Cross and Blue Shield, one of the biggest insurers of last resort in the United States, said its board had approved the proposal and would hold public hearings on the matter.
"Given current market conditions, we believe we have no choice but to take this step," Dr. Michael Stocker, the company's president and chief executive, said in a statement.
"This plan serves our mission to provide charitable services and ensures our growth in this new competitive marketplace."

If approved, the proposed conversion would give the company entry to public capital markets and allow it to compete against for-profit healthcare insurers and managed-care organisations, the company said.
"Health plans need large amounts of capital to acquire the latest technology and form partnerships with top-flight doctors and hospitals," Empire said in announcing its proposal.
About a half dozen Blue Cross firms in other states have already converted either partly or completely into for-profit companies.

The 60-year-old New York company said its proposal "avoids many of the pitfalls experienced by other Blue Cross and Blue Shield plans." Among them were disputes over control of the new companies and compensation for top executives.
Under its plan, Empire would transfer its assets, liabilities and business to its existing for-profit subsidiaries.
The organisation would then convert to a nonprofit foundation or create a new foundation that would own 100 percent of the stock of the for-profit subsidiary.
The foundation would sell some of the for-profit subsidiary's stock to the public, Empire said.
Over five years, the foundation would sell at least 95 percent of the for-profit subsidiary's equity and use the cash for charitable purposes.
Empire said the nonprofit foundation would have its own directors and operate under a new name.

"The independent for-profit company would carry on business under the Empire Blue Cross and Blue Shield name and conduct a second public offering of stock at some point in the future to raise funds in the capital market," Empire said.
No managers or directors would benefit financially from the transactions, it added.

Empire said final details of the proposal have yet to be fixed, pending public hearings and consultations with state regulators. Some terms of the plan must also be approved by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Empire said.
